title: The Comedy of Errors
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Ephesus, a trading city on the coast of Asia Minor, in the course of a single day
lengthNote: Around 1,777 lines — the shortest play in the canon
openingLine: Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall And by the doom of death end woes and all.
summary: Two sets of identical twins, separated as infants in a shipwreck, end up in the same city on the same day without knowing it. For five acts the wrong master beats the wrong servant, the wrong husband is locked out of his own dinner, and a gold chain, a purse and a length of rope travel between people who each believe the other has gone mad. Shakespeare doubles Plautus’s one pair of twins into two, which quadruples the mistakes, and then wraps the whole machine in a story of an old man under sentence of death who has spent five years looking for his family. The farce is timed to the hour; the frame is timed to a lifetime.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Comedy of Errors
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Prose passages are numbered by printed line, so modern editions vary by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Early enough to be among the first comedies, and certainly in existence by the Gray’s Inn performance of December 1594.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto. The First Folio text is the only early one, and it is unusually clean.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare adds a second pair of twins from Plautus’s Amphitruo, and the shipwrecked family from the old tale of Apollonius of Tyre.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The action runs from the morning of Aegeon’s trial to the five o’clock hour set for his execution.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A death sentence, and a stranger in town
structure.summary: Aegeon, a merchant of Syracuse, is condemned to die by sunset under a law he did not know existed, and tells the Duke how a shipwreck split his family in two. Within minutes his surviving son walks into the same city looking for the lost half, hands his money to a servant who looks exactly like his own, and is told by the wrong Dromio that his wife is waiting for dinner.

scenes.title: The trial
scenes.summary: Aegeon tells the story of the wreck, the split family and the five-year search, and is given until five o’clock to raise a thousand marks.

scenes.title: The wrong Dromio
scenes.summary: Antipholus of Syracuse gives his purse to his Dromio, is met by the other, and beats him for talking about a wife and a dinner.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The wife claims the wrong husband
structure.summary: Adriana waits for a husband who is late, argues with her sister about whether wives should wait at all, and then finds him in the street — except that it is his twin, who has never seen her. She sweeps him in to dinner. He decides he is either dreaming or in a city of witches, and goes along with it.

scenes.title: Liberty
scenes.summary: Adriana and Luciana debate a husband’s freedom; the Ephesian Dromio reports being beaten for delivering a dinner invitation.

scenes.title: The elm and the vine
scenes.summary: Adriana reproaches the Syracusan Antipholus as her estranged husband and takes him home; he agrees to be whoever they think he is.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Locked out, and wooing the wrong sister
structure.summary: Antipholus of Ephesus brings guests home and is refused entry to his own house by a servant he cannot see, while his double eats his dinner inside. Rather than break the door down in public, he goes off to the Courtesan. Indoors, the visiting twin has fallen in love with his supposed wife’s sister, and his Dromio has been claimed by the kitchen-maid.

scenes.title: The door
scenes.summary: The Ephesian Antipholus and his guests are kept out of his house by the Syracusan Dromio, who is inside; he decides to dine elsewhere and give the Courtesan the gold chain meant for his wife.

scenes.title: Luciana and the globe
scenes.summary: The Syracusan Antipholus courts Luciana, who thinks he is her brother-in-law; his Dromio describes the kitchen-maid as a globe; Angelo hands over the chain to the wrong man.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Arrests, a rope, and an exorcist
structure.summary: Money now chases the errors. Angelo wants payment for the chain and has the Ephesian Antipholus arrested for a debt he never incurred; the bail money is fetched by the wrong Dromio and given to the wrong master. Adriana, convinced her husband is possessed, hires Doctor Pinch to bind him, and the Syracusan pair conclude the whole city is enchanted.

scenes.title: The arrest
scenes.summary: Angelo demands his money; the Ephesian Antipholus, who never received the chain, is arrested for debt and sends his Dromio — the wrong one — for bail.

scenes.title: Time the bankrupt
scenes.summary: Luciana tells Adriana about the wooing; the Syracusan Dromio arrives for bail money with a riddling speech about the sergeant and Time.

scenes.title: Everyone knows my name
scenes.summary: The Syracusan Antipholus is greeted, thanked and given goods by strangers; the Courtesan asks for her chain and is taken for the devil.

scenes.title: Doctor Pinch
scenes.summary: The Ephesian Antipholus is brought a rope instead of money, declared possessed and bound; the Syracusan pair appear with swords and scatter everyone.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Sanctuary, and both pairs on stage at once
structure.summary: The Syracusan twins take refuge in a priory whose Abbess refuses to hand them over. As the Duke leads Aegeon to execution, both Antipholuses and both Dromios are finally in the same place, and what has been impossible to explain becomes obvious to look at. The Abbess turns out to be Aegeon’s wife, the fine is waived, and the two Dromios leave together.

scenes.title: The priory
scenes.summary: The Abbess lectures Adriana on jealousy and keeps her guests; the Duke hears every party’s contradictory story until the second pair walks in; Aemilia recognises her husband, and the family is put back together.

characters.name: Antipholus of Syracuse
characters.role: The travelling twin, searching for his mother and brother
characters.summary: He arrives in Ephesus knowing he is incomplete — a drop of water looking for another drop — and the city obligingly hands him a wife, a dinner, a chain and a name. He is the only person on stage who suspects a supernatural explanation, and the only one whose bewilderment is voiced in verse rather than blows.
characters.clue: A traveller who calls himself a drop of water, gets a free dinner from a wife he has never met, and falls in love with her sister.

relationships.label: twin brother of
relationships.note: They do not meet until the last hundred lines.

characters.name: Antipholus of Ephesus
characters.role: The settled twin, a citizen of Ephesus with a house, a wife and a reputation
characters.summary: He does not appear until Act III, by which time his life has been quietly taken over. The play makes him the twin who has everything and loses it all in an afternoon: his door, his dinner, his chain, his credit and finally his liberty, bound and carried off as a lunatic. He answers every loss with anger, which is exactly what the errors need.
characters.clue: Locked out of his own house while his dinner is eaten inside, arrested for a chain he never got, and tied up by an exorcist before tea.

relationships.label: former soldier under, and petitioner to

characters.name: Dromio of Syracuse
characters.summary: The wittier Dromio, whose set-piece geography of the kitchen-maid’s body is the longest joke in the play. He is the first to decide that Ephesus is fairyland and the first to reach for a Christian cross when it seems so; his fear is comic because it is also the most reasonable response anyone has.
characters.clue: A servant who maps the countries of the world on a kitchen-maid, and begs his master to leave a town full of witches.

characters.name: Dromio of Ephesus
characters.summary: He is beaten in the first act for delivering a true message to the wrong man, and spends the play keeping a tally of blows on his own skin. He is sent for a rope and returns to find his master wanting bail money, and never once gets a straight answer. His last lines, offered to his newly found twin, are the gentlest in the play.
characters.clue: Sent for a rope’s end, paid in blows, and the last to speak: he offers to walk out hand in hand with his brother rather than argue about who is the elder.

characters.name: Adriana
characters.summary: Shakespeare’s addition to Plautus, where the wife is a nag without a name. Adriana has a name, a grievance and a theory of marriage in which two people are one body, which is why a husband who acts like a stranger feels to her like a self-mutilation. The Abbess blames her jealousy for everything; the play has shown us it was not jealousy but accurate observation of the wrong man.
characters.clue: She calls her husband an elm and herself a vine, drags the wrong twin home to dinner, and is scolded by an abbess for a jealousy the audience knows was well-founded.
traits: wronged in a way nobody can explain

characters.name: Luciana
characters.summary: She preaches patience and wifely obedience in Act II and is then courted, in Act III, by the man she takes to be her sister’s husband. Her advice to him — if you must be false, be discreet about it — is the play’s most uncomfortable line, and her silence when the truth comes out leaves the promised marriage entirely to the audience’s imagination.
characters.clue: She tells her sister that a man is master of his liberty, then finds herself being wooed by the husband she was defending.

characters.name: Aegeon
characters.role: A merchant of Syracuse, father of the Antipholus twins
characters.summary: He opens the play asking to be executed, and his hundred-line account of the shipwreck is the longest piece of narrative in any Shakespeare comedy. He then vanishes until the last scene, where his own son fails to recognise him. The farce runs inside the hours he has been given to live, and productions that keep him visible remind the audience of that clock.
characters.clue: An old man given until five o’clock to find a thousand marks, who tells the whole story of the shipwreck before anyone else has spoken.

characters.name: Aemilia, the Abbess
characters.role: Abbess of the priory in Ephesus; Aegeon’s lost wife
characters.summary: She appears only in the last scene, and in a hundred lines takes charge of it: refusing Adriana entry, diagnosing the husband’s madness as the wife’s fault, and then recognising the condemned man as her own husband. Her presence turns Plautine farce into a family romance, and she is the only person who ends the play having found more than she lost.
characters.clue: A holy woman who shelters the fugitives, lectures a wife on jealousy, and turns out to have been searching for the same family as everyone else.

characters.name: Duke Solinus
characters.summary: A ruler who enforces a law he openly regrets, and who spends the last scene as a judge trying to reconcile four sworn statements that cannot all be true. He is the audience’s stand-in in Act V: he hears everything and understands nothing until the twins stand side by side, at which point he says what everybody is thinking.
characters.clue: He sentences a stranger to death in the first scene, and in the last cannot tell which of two identical men is the spirit and which the natural man.

characters.name: Doctor Pinch
characters.summary: Hired to exorcise the Ephesian Antipholus, he takes one look and pronounces both master and man possessed. He has fewer than twenty lines and is later reported singed, shorn and doused, which is the play’s only revenge on the profession of explaining things.
characters.clue: A thin conjurer who diagnoses possession by the paleness of a face, and has his beard set alight for his trouble.

themes.name: Identity, and what proves it
themes.summary: Nobody in Ephesus can prove who they are, because everything that usually does the job — a face, a name, a servant, a wife, a signature on a bill — belongs equally to somebody else. The play asks what is left of a person once the world stops confirming them, and the Syracusan twin’s answer is to give up and be whoever he is told he is.
themes.development: In 1.2 identity is a lack (a drop seeking a drop); by 2.2 it is a costume to be worn as directed; in 5.1 it is settled by the only evidence that works, two bodies side by side.

themes.name: Marriage and its double standard
themes.summary: Adriana and Luciana hold the play’s one real argument: whether a husband’s liberty should be greater than a wife’s. Luciana says it should; the plot then hands her sister a husband who behaves like a stranger, an Abbess who blames the wife, and a courtesan with the dinner ring. The comedy never resolves the argument, it only ends it.
themes.development: Debated in 2.1, dramatised in 2.2 with the elm and the vine, and judged against Adriana in 5.1 by a woman who has been a nun for thirty-three years.

themes.name: Time and the deadline
themes.summary: The play is one of two in the canon that keep the unity of time, and it keeps it with a death sentence. Every act is closer to five o’clock. Dromio’s riddles about Time as a bald bankrupt and a thief are jokes, but they are the play’s jokes: the clock is what the errors are racing.
themes.development: Set at 1.1 with the Duke’s deadline, mocked in 2.2 and 4.2 by Dromio, and reached in 5.1 as the executioner’s hour becomes the family’s reunion.

themes.name: Evidence and the failure of proof
themes.summary: The last act is a trial in which every witness is honest and every testimony contradicts the others. Chains, purses, rings and dinner-times are produced as proof and prove nothing, because each fact is true of a different man. The play is a small demonstration that evidence depends on the assumption of one body per name.
themes.development: Small misreadings in Acts I–II become legal ones in Act IV (arrest for debt) and a formal hearing in Act V, resolved by sight rather than argument.

themes.name: Warts, spunk-water and signs
themes.summary: Ephesus was the city of sorcerers in the Acts of the Apostles, and the Syracusan visitors arrive already primed to see witchcraft. Their explanation for the day — enchantment, goblins, a devil in the shape of a courtesan — is wrong, but it is also the only theory anybody offers that fits all the facts. Doctor Pinch, brought in to exorcise the Ephesian twin, applies the same theory from the other side.
themes.development: A rumour in 1.2, a conviction by 2.2 and 3.2, a formal exorcism in 4.4, and quietly dropped in 5.1 when the natural explanation walks on.

techniques.name: Identical twins
techniques.definition: A plot device by which one actor's part is doubled by another body.
techniques.inThisBook: Two pairs rather than Plautus’s one, so that mistakes can run master-to-servant as well as brother-to-brother; the pairs are kept apart until 5.1, when the audience finally sees what it has been imagining.

techniques.name: Farce structure
techniques.definition: Symmetrical plotting in which two of everything collide.
techniques.inThisBook: Each error is generated by the last and cleared by the next: a purse, a chain, a rope and a bail-fee circulate through the wrong hands in strict order, and the timing is exact enough to run as a musical.

techniques.name: The classical unities
techniques.definition: Keeping a play to one place, one day and one action.
techniques.inThisBook: One city, one day between a sentence and an execution, and one street with three doors — the priory, the Phoenix and the Porpentine — which a Gray’s Inn audience trained on Roman comedy would have recognised at once.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: The audience is told about both sets of twins in the first scene, and from then on holds the one fact that would end the play; every scene of rage and bewilderment is comic only because of it.

techniques.name: Retrospective exposition
techniques.definition: Putting the backstory into a single long scene of telling rather than showing.
techniques.inThisBook: Aegeon’s speech in 1.1 delivers the shipwreck, the separation and the search in a hundred lines of verse before any twin appears — the same device Shakespeare returns to for Prospero at the start of The Tempest.

techniques.name: Objects that change hands
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: The gold chain is ordered, delivered, denied, demanded and produced in court; the rope’s end is fetched as bail money. Every object is proof of something, and the errors are the objects moving one pair of hands to the left.

quotations.text: Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall And by the doom of death end woes and all.
quotations.speaker: Aegeon
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play, addressed to the Duke who has just condemned him.
quotations.analysis: A comedy begins with a man asking to be executed, in a rhymed couplet, which is a strange key to open in. The couplet is the point: Aegeon has already made a finished shape of his life, and the play’s job is to break it open again. Everything that follows happens inside the hours he has been given.

quotations.text: Hopeless and helpless doth AEgeon wend, But to procrastinate his lifeless end.
quotations.speaker: Aegeon
quotations.context: Leaving the stage under guard, with a day to find a thousand marks.
quotations.analysis: He refers to himself in the third person, as a chronicle would, and ‘procrastinate’ carries its old sense of putting off rather than idling. The couplet is a stage exit that also dismisses him from the play for four acts; the farce goes on in the time he is spending.

quotations.text: I to the world am like a drop of water That in the ocean seeks another drop, Who, falling there to find his fellow forth, Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself:
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Alone in Ephesus, having sent his servant to the inn, thinking of the brother and mother he is looking for.
quotations.analysis: The image predicts what the play will do to him. To find his fellow drop he must fall into the ocean, and there he ‘confounds himself’ — loses his outline exactly as the city is about to make him lose his name. Adriana will use the same image of a drop in the gulf in 2.2, meaning marriage, without knowing she is quoting the wrong man’s thought back at him.

quotations.text: They say this town is full of cozenage, As, nimble jugglers that deceive the eye, Dark-working sorcerers that change the mind, Soul-killing witches that deform the body, Disguised cheaters, prating mountebanks, And many such-like liberties of sin:
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: After the Ephesian Dromio has denied all knowledge of the money he was given.
quotations.analysis: The catalogue is arranged by target — eye, mind, body — as though he were consulting a manual. Ephesus had this reputation from the Acts of the Apostles, where its citizens burn their magic books, and the speech shows a visitor arriving with the explanation ready before the evidence. For the rest of the play he will fit every fact to it.

quotations.text: Why should their liberty than ours be more?
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: To Luciana, who has just said that a man is master of his liberty.
quotations.analysis: A single line of question against three lines of her sister’s proverb, and the question is never answered — Luciana replies that men’s business lies out of doors, which is a description rather than a reason. The exchange is Shakespeare’s addition to Plautus, and it gives the play a real disagreement about marriage before the farce has any need of one.

quotations.text: How comes it now, my husband, O, how comes it, That thou art thus estranged from thyself?
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: In the street, to the Syracusan Antipholus, whom she takes for her husband.
quotations.analysis: She has the diagnosis exactly right and the patient exactly wrong: the man in front of her is estranged from her husband’s self because he is not her husband. The doubled ‘how comes it’ is a wife’s bewilderment, and the word ‘estranged’ is doing double duty, since the stranger really is one.

quotations.text: For know, my love, as easy mayest thou fall A drop of water in the breaking gulf, And take unmingled that same drop again, Without addition or diminishing, As take from me thyself and not me too.
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: Arguing that husband and wife are one substance and cannot be separated.
quotations.analysis: Her image of marriage is the same image of a drop in the sea that the Syracusan twin used of himself in 1.2 — but there the drop was searching and here it is dissolved. The two speeches use one figure for opposite things, loss of a brother and union with a husband, and the man listening has heard both without knowing it.

quotations.text: Thou art an elm, my husband, I a vine, Whose weakness, married to thy stronger state, Makes me with thy strength to communicate:
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: Taking the arm of the man she believes is her husband and leading him in to dinner.
quotations.analysis: The elm and vine is a classical emblem of marriage, from Virgil and Ovid, and she uses it while physically fastening on his sleeve — the figure and the gesture are the same. She makes herself the weak vine in the sentence, but she is the one doing the leading, and the ‘elm’ goes in to dinner because he cannot think of a reason not to.

quotations.text: This is the fairy land: O spite of spites! We talk with goblins, owls and sprites: If we obey them not, this will ensue, They'll suck our breath, or pinch us black and blue.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: After Adriana and Luciana have claimed him and his master as their own household.
quotations.analysis: The line falls into rhymed short verse, the metre Shakespeare gives fairies in the Dream, as if Dromio’s fear had changed the play’s form for four lines. ‘Pinch us black and blue’ is what fairies do to sinners in folklore, and what Doctor Pinch, of all names, will try to do to the other twin in Act IV.

quotations.text: Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell? Sleeping or waking? mad or well-advised? Known unto these, and to myself disguised!
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Alone for a moment, after being claimed as husband and invited to dinner.
quotations.analysis: Three questions, each a pair of opposites, and he cannot settle any of them; the third line resolves the problem by giving up. ‘Known unto these, and to myself disguised’ inverts the usual comedy of disguise, where a character knows who they are and others do not — here everyone else is certain and he is the one in the dark.

quotations.text: Say what you will, sir, but I know what I know; That you beat me at the mart, I have your hand to show: If the skin were parchment, and the blows you gave were ink, Your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: To his master, who denies having beaten him that morning — because it was the other Antipholus who did.
quotations.analysis: Dromio offers his own skin as a legal document, and the joke has a serious edge: in this play the body is the only record that cannot be forged. The long rhymed lines — fourteeners, an old-fashioned metre by 1594 — give the servant a jog-trot ballad voice that sits against his master’s blank verse.

quotations.text: Sweet mistress--what your name is else, I know not, Nor by what wonder you do hit of mine,--
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: To Luciana, who has just begged him to be kinder to her sister and, if he must be unfaithful, to be discreet.
quotations.analysis: He begins a love-speech by admitting he does not know her name, which is the one thing a lover in a sonnet always knows. The dashes and the broken syntax are the sound of a man wooing while genuinely confused, and the scene’s quatrains — the only rhymed wooing in the play — are addressed to the one person in Ephesus who thinks he belongs to somebody else.

quotations.text: she is spherical, like a globe; I could find out countries in her.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: Describing the kitchen-maid who has claimed him as her husband.
quotations.analysis: What follows is a tour of Europe conducted on a woman’s body — Ireland, Scotland, France, Spain, the Indies — and it is the longest single joke in the play. A globe was a newish object in the 1590s, and the routine treats a servant’s fear of being married as a piece of cartography; the map is funny, and it is also how the play’s people keep turning each other into things.

quotations.text: Time is a very bankrupt, and owes more than he's worth, to season.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: To Adriana, who has asked why he says the hour has gone back.
quotations.analysis: The riddle is that a sergeant arresting a debtor makes the clock seem to run backwards. Time as a bankrupt is a joke, but a play with a five o’clock execution cannot afford jokes about time being in debt: Dromio is describing the thing the whole plot is racing, and doing it in the language of the arrest that has just happened offstage.

quotations.text: There's not a man I meet but doth salute me As if I were their well-acquainted friend; And every one doth call me by my name.
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Alone, wearing a gold chain he did not order, after being thanked and offered goods by strangers.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is that everyone knows him — which is also exactly what a man searching for his family has wanted. The play’s cruelty is that recognition arrives before he can accept it, so being called by his name feels like sorcery rather than homecoming. He is wearing the chain as he speaks, and that will be evidence against his brother within the hour.

quotations.text: Mistress, both man and master is possess'd; I know it by their pale and deadly looks: They must be bound and laid in some dark room.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Pinch
quotations.context: Diagnosing the Ephesian Antipholus and his Dromio after they have contradicted everyone present.
quotations.analysis: The verb is singular for two patients — ‘man and master is’ — as if the two had already been bundled into one case. The dark room is what Malvolio gets in Twelfth Night, and both plays make the same point: a community that cannot explain a man’s behaviour will call it madness and lock the door. Pinch is the only person to claim expertise, and he is wrong about everything.

quotations.text: The venom clamours of a jealous woman Poisons more deadly than a mad dog's tooth.
quotations.speaker: Aemilia, the Abbess
quotations.context: To Adriana, having drawn from her an admission that she nagged her husband.
quotations.analysis: The Abbess has led Adriana through a set of questions like a cross-examiner and then delivers the verdict: the wife’s complaints drove the husband mad. The audience knows the madness was two men in one name, so the sentence lands as a piece of stern, plausible and completely mistaken wisdom — and it is spoken by the one woman who, in a few minutes, will turn out to be the mother of both husbands.

quotations.text: One of these men is Genius to the other; And so of these. Which is the natural man, And which the spirit? who deciphers them?
quotations.speaker: Duke Solinus
quotations.context: As both Antipholuses and both Dromios stand on stage together for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The Duke’s first thought is not ‘twins’ but ‘a man and his attendant spirit’ — the supernatural explanation the Syracusans have held all along, now offered by the sanest person in the play. ‘Who deciphers them?’ treats the four men as a text to be read, which is what the audience has been doing for five acts; the difference is that the audience had the key.

quotations.text: Thirty-three years have I but gone in travail Of you, my sons; and till this present hour My heavy burden ne'er delivered.
quotations.speaker: Aemilia, the Abbess
quotations.context: Inviting everyone into the priory for a feast, once husband and sons are recognised.
quotations.analysis: She describes the whole separation as one long labour, so that the reunion is a birth and the play’s single day is the day of delivery. It is a mother’s image and also a nun’s; the ‘heavy burden’ is both. The line gives the farce a second clock, running underneath the Duke’s: not the hours to five, but the years to now.

quotations.text: Methinks you are my glass, and not my brother: I see by you I am a sweet-faced youth.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: The two Dromios, left alone on stage after everyone else has gone in.
quotations.analysis: The first thing a man does with a newly found twin is use him as a mirror, and the compliment is to himself. It is the gentlest joke in the play because it reverses everything that has gone before: for five acts, being taken for the other Dromio meant a beating, and now it means finding out he is good-looking.

quotations.text: We came into the world like brother and brother; And now let's go hand in hand, not one before another.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, after the brothers have argued briefly about who is the elder and should go first.
quotations.analysis: Shakespeare gives the final couplet to the servants, not to the Duke or the reunited husband and wife, and the couplet is about refusing a hierarchy. Every scene so far has depended on people going in and out of doors in the wrong order; the last exit is taken side by side, and the long loose rhymed lines let the two of them amble off rather than march.

timeline.label: Performed at Gray’s Inn on 28 December — the ‘Night of Errors’
timeline.detail: The Gesta Grayorum records a play called The Comedy of Errors staged at the Inn’s Christmas revels, after an evening of such confusion that the night was named for it.

timeline.label: William Warner’s English translation of Plautus’s Menaechmi printed
timeline.detail: The first English version of Shakespeare’s main source appears in print a year after the play was already on stage; he seems to have worked from the Latin.

timeline.label: Francis Meres lists ‘his Errors’ among Shakespeare’s comedies
timeline.detail: Palladis Tamia names the play among the works that made Shakespeare, in Meres’s view, the English Plautus.

timeline.label: Performed at court on 28 December
timeline.detail: A second Innocents’ Day performance, ten years after the first, this time before James I.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, placed fifth among the comedies. No quarto was ever printed.

timeline.label: See If You Like It; or, ’Tis All a Mistake
timeline.detail: An eighteenth-century adaptation that sold the play on its confusion rather than its author.

timeline.label: Thomas Hull’s The Twins
timeline.detail: Another reworking, retitled around the doubling device; the play survived the century largely through such alterations.

timeline.label: Samuel Phelps revives the play at Sadler’s Wells
timeline.detail: Part of Phelps’s campaign to return Shakespeare’s own texts to the London stage.

timeline.label: The Boys from Syracuse opens on Broadway
timeline.detail: Rodgers and Hart’s musical, directed by George Abbott, keeps the twins and drops the title.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn’s RSC musical version
timeline.detail: Music by Guy Woolfenden, choreography by Gillian Lynne, Judi Dench as Adriana; it transferred to the Aldwych and was filmed for television in 1978.

timeline.label: BBC Television Shakespeare
timeline.detail: James Cellan Jones’s production, with Michael Kitchen and Roger Daltrey as the twins and a map of Ephesus for a floor.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: The city of the play: a port of merchants, goldsmiths and a priory, with a reputation for sorcery inherited from the Acts of the Apostles.

places.name: Syracuse
places.note: Aegeon’s home city, at war with Ephesus in trade; a Syracusan found in Ephesus dies unless he can pay a thousand marks.

places.name: Epidamnum
places.note: Modern Durrës in Albania, where Aegeon’s wife bore the twins and where the family set sail into the storm that divided them.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Fishermen of Corinth took Aemilia and one twin from the wreck; the Ephesian Antipholus was raised there before coming to the Duke’s service.

places.name: Gray’s Inn, London
places.note: Where the play was performed at the Christmas revels of 1594, on a night remembered for its own confusion.

criticalViews.position: Farce, and a very good one
criticalViews.summary: The oldest view treats the play as an exercise in Plautine mechanism, brilliantly timed and not much more: a young dramatist showing that he can run two pairs of twins through one door faster than his model ran one.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away Aegeon, the Abbess and the verse of Adriana and the Syracusan twin, none of which farce requires and all of which Shakespeare added.

criticalViews.summary: A reading that takes the frame seriously: the shipwreck, the separated family and the recognition at the priory belong to the same tradition as Pericles and The Winter’s Tale, and the errors are the comic middle of a story about loss and recovery.
criticalViews.counter: Aegeon is offstage for four acts, and the reunion, however moving, is delivered in under a hundred lines; the play spends its time on the mistakes, not the grief.

criticalViews.position: A play about the loss of self
criticalViews.summary: Modern criticism has been drawn to the Syracusan twin’s language of dissolution and disguise, and to Adriana’s theory of marriage as shared substance: the comedy is read as an anxious experiment in what happens when a name stops belonging to one body.
criticalViews.counter: The anxiety is real but it is confined to two characters; the Ephesian twin and both Dromios experience the day as an outrage, not as a crisis of identity.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare make the audience’s knowledge the source of the comedy?
essayQuestions.focus: Dramatic irony and the design of the errors
plan: Begin with 1.1: the audience is given the whole family history before any twin appears, which is the opposite of a mystery.
Trace one object — the chain — from Angelo’s workshop to the Duke’s hearing, showing how each mistake is comic only because the audience can see where it went.
Contrast the two Antipholuses’ responses: the visitor suspects witchcraft, the citizen suspects conspiracy, and both are reasonable without the audience’s key.
Use 5.1 to show the Duke, the last person to know, standing in for a spectator who has arrived without the first scene.
Conclude on what the play gains and loses by never once letting a character on stage share what the audience knows.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Adriana is a jealous wife.’ How far does the play agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Marriage, the double standard and the Abbess
plan: Set out the 2.1 debate: Luciana’s argument for patience against Adriana’s question about liberty, and note that the question is never answered.
Read the elm-and-vine speech in 2.2 as a theory of marriage rather than a complaint, and notice that it is delivered to the wrong man.
Weigh the evidence the play gives Adriana: a husband who is late, gives away her chain and dines with a courtesan — all true of the Ephesian twin.
Examine the Abbess’s cross-examination in 5.1, where the audience knows her verdict is wrong.
Decide whether the ending vindicates Adriana, corrects her, or simply moves on.

essayQuestions.question: Why does the play need Aegeon?
essayQuestions.focus: The romance frame and the unity of time
plan: Note that Plautus has no such character; the condemned father is Shakespeare’s addition from the Apollonius story.
Show how his sentence gives the play its clock: five o’clock is the hour the farce is running towards.
Consider what his long narrative in 1.1 does to the tone before the first joke.
Look at 5.1, where his own son denies knowing him, as the moment the errors stop being funny.
Argue for what a production loses by cutting him down, or gains by keeping him visible.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Ephesus as a place.
essayQuestions.focus: Money, law, sorcery and the city
plan: Open with the law of 1.1, which makes a trading city into a place where the wrong passport is a death sentence.
Gather the commerce: marks, ducats, a chain, a purse, bail — the errors are mostly errors of payment.
Set that against the Syracusan twin’s catalogue of jugglers and witches in 1.2, and ask why both descriptions fit.
Use Doctor Pinch and the priory to show a city with its own institutions for explaining madness.
Close on the last scene, where the city that would have executed a stranger feasts him instead.

discussionQuestions: Antipholus of Syracuse decides to go along with whatever he is told. Is that cowardice, curiosity or the only sane response?
The Abbess blames Adriana’s jealousy for her husband’s madness. Does the play expect us to agree with her?
Every error involves money or an object changing hands. What would the play lose if the mistakes were purely about faces?
The two Dromios get the last word. Why not the Duke, or the reunited parents?
How much darker could a production make Aegeon’s death sentence before the play stopped being a comedy?

related.why: Shakespeare’s other pair of separated twins, a decade later, with the mistaken identities turned towards love rather than debt.
The only other play in the canon to keep the unity of time, and another that opens with a long speech of backstory.
The same shipwreck-and-reunion story of Apollonius of Tyre, treated as romance rather than as the frame for a farce.
An early comedy from the same years, equally interested in what a wife is expected to put up with.
Lovers who wake up attached to the wrong partner, and fairies who really do pinch people black and blue.
